planting.note: Set out only after nights stay above 55°F; in marginal zones grow in a large container and overwinter indoors near a bright window.

directions: Grown chiefly for its striking two-lobed leaves, which are shaped like an outstretched bat or moth wing and mottled with silvery-green markings; the small greenish-yellow flowers are fragrant but modest compared to the foliage. Provide a trellis or arbor in filtered light with rich, well-drained soil, since intense afternoon sun can scorch the thin leaves in hot climates. It serves as a larval host for several Heliconius (longwing) butterflies, making it a favorite addition to tropical butterfly houses and shaded pollinator gardens. Pinch young vines to encourage branching and mulch the root zone, since top growth dies back quickly below 40°F even though the crown may resprout.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Transplant once soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; site along a fence or shrub the vine can scramble through.

directions: A slender, fast-growing vine named for its habit of producing small creamy-white flowers in pairs at each leaf node, followed by pea-sized dark purple fruit. The distinctive three-lobed leaves resemble a shallow trident and readily distinguish it from other dooryard passionvines. It is a favored larval host for Gulf Fritillary, Zebra Longwing, and Julia butterflies along the Gulf Coast, so allow some foliage loss to caterpillars rather than spraying. Grow on a low trellis, fence, or through open shrubs in full sun; plants tolerate light, sandy soils and rebound quickly from occasional hard pruning.

planting.note: Start seed indoors well ahead of the frost-free date; transplant to a permanent, wind-sheltered site only in frost-free conditions.

directions: Named for its glossy, laurel-like leaves, this vigorous tropical vine bears fragrant lavender-and-white flowers followed by egg-shaped, orange-yellow fruit filled with juicy, translucent, sweet-tart arils prized fresh or blended into drinks throughout the Caribbean and northern South America. It requires a strong, permanent trellis or arbor since mature vines are heavy and long-lived, and it is intolerant of any frost, making it best suited to true tropical or protected coastal conditions. Provide rich, well-drained soil and consistent moisture during fruit development, and hand-pollinate where natural pollinators are scarce to improve fruit set. Harvest fruit as it colors fully and begins to soften near the stem end.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Best where summer nights stay cool; in hot, humid climates provide afternoon shade and excellent air circulation to reduce fungal disease.

directions: An Andean cloud-forest species valued for its spectacular pendant, tubular scarlet-red flowers that draw hummingbirds, followed by elongated yellow-orange, banana-shaped fruit with sweet aromatic pulp. Unlike lowland tropical Passiflora, it performs best with cool nights and moderate summer heat, so gardeners outside its native highland range should site it with afternoon shade and grow it against a sturdy trellis with excellent drainage. It is markedly less heat- and humidity-tolerant than Passiflora edulis, and prolonged temperatures above the mid-90s°F can cause bud drop, so a shaded, breezy location extends its usefulness in warm-summer gardens. Mulch heavily and protect the root zone in any winter approaching freezing, since top growth is damaged well above the hardiness limits of hardier native passionflowers.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products
